articles.title: ‘The angle of the dog, the hat and the tattoo on her foot all come together’: Trace Meek’s best phone picture
articles.summary: A family day in a Florida back yard was the setting for a summertime memory it would be impossible to recreate. Trace Meek is abundantly proud of his Florida back yard. For the last 10 years, he and his wife, Lauren, have worked diligently on it. “It’s our happy place,” he says.
body: The family had friends visiting for 4 July celebrations when Meek took this photo on his phone. There were six adults, six children and two dogs present. Harvey, a braque français, is pictured here on Lauren’s lap.
“Harvey was four at the time. He loves to swim, and had been jumping in the pool all day, but eventually tired and climbed on to Lauren’s lap to rest,” Meek says.

Re-enacting the shot would be almost impossible, he adds, but “that’s the cool part. The angle of the dog, the hat and the cup, the tattoo on her foot, along with the vibrant colours of the raft – it all comes together. I love how the water creates shapes, too. You have to really study the image to see what it’s about.”

Lauren’s face being covered by her hat lends an air of mysteriousness that Meek also enjoys. “You can put yourself in her place and be immersed in a wonderful summertime memory; a moment when you were truly content.”
points: A family day in a Florida back yard was the setting for a summertime memory it would be impossible to recreate.

articles.title: Adele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’
articles.summary: The author on the habit she can’t control, the writer she’s never read, and the true love of her life (it’s not her husband) Born in North Yorkshire, Adele Parks, 57, studied English at the University of Leicester then worked in advertising.
body: What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? Speaking negatively to myself.

What was your most embarrassing moment? When I concentrate, I put my thumb in my mouth. I once did it during a really important meeting when asked a question I didn’t know the answer to. When I left the meeting my friend said: “What did you put your thumb in your mouth for?” I didn’t know I’d done it.
What would your superpower be? Teleportation – but with clothes. I don’t want to turn up anywhere naked.
What makes you unhappy? Hopelessness – when people have stopped believing they can improve or a situation can improve.

articles.title: The hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on it | Max Liu
articles.summary: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing. “If you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.” It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me. Barbecues are one of life’s perennial disappointments.
body: I grew up in Cornwall, where beach barbecues were a rite of passage. The flame under the sandy grill was blown out by the Atlantic wind, so these gatherings were impractical, unpredictable and interminable. One minute the sausages were raw and looked like they’d never be ready, the next they were hard and black and basically inedible. Rain frequently sent us scrambling to pack up and flee for shelter.

The popularity of barbecues is inexplicable yet undeniable, with black smoke puffing from back gardens at the first sniff of a sunny day. When I broached my hatred with an Australian, she reacted as if I wanted to deprive her of her birthright. But just because people keep doing something doesn’t necessarily mean they actually enjoy it.

Barbecues are antisocial in other, more important ways. I used to live above a man who liked to come home from work and barbecue steak on his patio, directly below my kitchen. I had to close every window to stop my whole flat stinking of beef. If you live in a densely populated area, it’s not particularly socially conscious to fill the air with meaty smog during hot weather, just so you can clog your arteries.
points: Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing.
“If you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.
It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me.

articles.title: Flipping marvellous: Yotam Ottolenghi on the joy of simple breakfasts – plus six exclusive recipes
articles.summary: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over. Forget fussing and focus on just one big lovely thing for the middle of the table. Here’s how. Family life has had a bigger impact on how I cook at home than almost anything else.
body: My weekend pancakes – which made their way into my book Simple Too – are supposed to be a batch-cooking exercise: lots made on Sunday, then reheated through the week, in the toaster or a dry pan on the stove, so breakfast is more or less solved until Friday. That’s the theory. In practice, all 22 pancakes the recipe makes are gone by Sunday lunch – eaten by the boys, their friends, or whoever happens to be over for breakfast.

But my kitchen on a weekend morning doesn’t only answer to my kids, even though that’s their indisputable assumption. I love having friends over for brunch, and what I actually want, most weeks, is one big thing in the middle of the table – generously for everyone. So they can help themselves and I’m not the only one standing after everyone else has sat down.

Like the butter beans with Urfa chilli butter, with toast, bacon and semi-hard-boiled eggs. Or a big tray of baked za’atar tomatoes and mascarpone, with some sausages and sourdough. Or a big pan of menemen (Turkish scrambled eggs) with a leaf salad and a few slices of avocado.
points: Weekend mornings are for family – and whoever happens to be over.

articles.title: What Would a ‘How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days’ Sequel Even Be About? 5 Predictions
articles.summary: “I want dating apps, I want ghosting, I want breadcrumbing, I want that thing where you arrange a drink with someone even though you really can’t be bothered and would rather be at home eating a posh lasagna for one.”
body: Another day, another millennial-nostalgia-baiting sequel to a classic late 1990s or early 2000s movie. This year alone we’ve had The Devil Wears Prada 2 and Practical Magic 2 —and now there are rumors of another afoot. Over the last week, it was reported that the 2003 rom-com How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, starring Kate Hudson and Matthew McConnaughey, may well be returning to screens for a part two.

In the original movie, Hudson plays Andie, a journalist writing an article about the most off-putting things women can do in relationships, while McConnaughey is Ben, an advertising exec who, for convoluted professional reasons, bets his colleagues that he can make any woman fall in love with him. Hijinks, as we know, very much ensue.

articles.title: Long Live the Hard Rock—Inside the Kitsch, Memorabilia, and Excess That Lives On
articles.summary: Writer Jessica Chapel on the memories and lore that keeps the brand iconic—and close to home.
body: I was about nine years old when my dad first took me to the Hard Rock Cafe in New York, and I still remember being completely taken with the walls. My dad and I gushed over everything together: That's Eddie Van Halen's suit—look, Jeff Ament's bass! There's no way that's Jimi Hendrix's actual handwriting. Of course, it's his signature, messy, cursive—a write-up of the classic track, Midnight Lightning. How about those massive, towering stage boots and custom bass guitars? Yep, they were used and worn by none other than Gene Simmons himself.

My dad was a rock ‘n’ roll traveler then, in the way some are food travelers today. Concerts determined where he went, and he had stories about bands the way others have stories about family vacations. We bonded deeply through music—so when we walked into a Hard Rock in any city, it wasn't simply a chain to me. Instead, it was a portal—filled with scents of hairspray, greasy burgers, and a touch of booze—that cosmically actualized the music so intrinsic to our relationship.
points: Writer Jessica Chapel on the memories and lore that keeps the brand iconic—and close to home.

articles.title: ‘Still or Sparkling’ Must Be Stopped
articles.summary: All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to release the pressure valve of crankiness that comes with sweating your way through the end of summer. This story was previously published as part of that series.
body: More and more often, my meal — even at ostensibly casual restaurants — begins not only with an attempted upsell, but with a question I’ve come to dread because of the weird stigma attached to my inevitable response.
You sit. Your server materializes. The question arrives: “Still or sparkling?” A beat. “Or filtered tap?”

It’s a strange way to begin an experience ostensibly centered on hospitality. Before I’ve had a chance to look at the menu, order a guava mezcal margarita, or even fully settle into my chair, I’m being asked whether I’d like to turn the most basic necessity on the table into a line item on the bill. Restaurants have plenty of opportunities to sell me things — that is, fundamentally, why I’m there — but surely the first sip of water can remain outside the machinery of the upsell.

articles.title: 8 Best Shampoos for Frizzy Hair, According to Hair Stylists and Vogue Editors
articles.summary: Can shampoo actually prevent hair frizz? Six pro hairstylists share everything you need to know; plus, shop Vogue’s edit of the best shampoos for frizzy hair.
body: After a trip to Puerto Vallarta this past June, I made a vow to myself: I will never again travel to a rainy, humid climate without a good shampoo for frizzy hair. Though the mountainous views were stunning, the state of my hair throughout my stay was not, and I spent my beach days in a tizzy of frizz.

Jackie Seabrooke, a celebrity hairstylist based in New York City, assured me that my hair nightmare was, alas, not unique. “When hair is dry and lacks moisture, it tries to absorb moisture from the air, causing the cuticle to swell and become frizzy,” she explained. “This is why hair tends to look even more frizzy in humid conditions.” But sometimes, unsightly frizz doesn’t even come with margaritas on the side.

Seabrooke said that even day-to-day activities—like washing with too-hot water, heat damage, rough towel drying, and genetics—can all play into hair that’s more staticky than silky. And though styling products can be a savior, frizz control starts in the shower.
points: Six pro hairstylists share everything you need to know; plus, shop Vogue’s edit of the best shampoos for frizzy hair.

articles.title: The Best NARS Products Have Serious Staying Power
articles.summary: The iconic ’90s beauty brand still holds up—in popularity and product wear time. From blush to foundation, these are the nine best NARS products according to Vogue.
body: For me, NARS is tied to some of my earliest memories of makeup. As a mid-’90s baby with a surprisingly sharp memory of my toddler years, I remember sneaking into my mom’s jade-green acrylic makeup case and pulling out products from the brand—including its iconic powder blushes with decidedly risqué names I was still too young to read.

While my own beauty bag options are much more varied, and my heavy-makeup phase as an alternative teenager may be behind me, there are still occasions that call for formulas capable of going the distance—say, the Met Gala. And while my relationship with makeup has changed considerably over the years, one thing has remained the same: blush is always a must.
